slides.text: Most poultry farms still feed and water their flock by hand.
slides.sub: It tires workers, takes time, and unmeasured feed means uneven portions for the hens.
slides.notes: Agriculture is the main livelihood of millions of Filipino families (PSA, 2023, as cited in Razonales et al., 2025). Chicken is the most common poultry because of its nutritional value and low cost (Eda et al., 2023). Feeding and watering practices affect its quality (Franco et al., 2020, as cited in Zhou et al., 2022). Most farms still do this manually, which leads to fatigue and inconsistent feed and water.

slides.title: A layer farm in San Pablo City, Laguna
slides.text: Laying hens are raised here for eggs. Workers check supplies, pour feed and look at the water several times a day.
slides.notes: The farm is in Barangay Del Remedio, San Pablo City. Layers need a nutrient-rich, consistent diet to sustain egg production.

slides.text: Reduce manual labor, minimize feed wastage and improve monitoring of feed and water.
slides.sub: For poultry farm owners in San Pablo City, through an automated system built on the Arduino Mega 2560 and the ESP32.
slides.notes: The general objective is to help poultry farm owners in San Pablo City, Laguna, improve their daily operations by designing and developing HyFePoul, which aims to reduce manual labor, minimize feed wastage, and provide better monitoring of feed and water availability.

slides.notes:
a. Implementing programmable feeding schedules of up to three daily feeding times, with an adjustable feed dispensing amount, set through the Nextion display or the mobile application and retained during power interruptions.
b. Distributing feed through a chain-driven moving hopper that travels along five feeding trays, using home and end limit switches to determine its starting and ending positions, prevent movement beyond its limits, and return home after each cycle.

slides.foot: From Chapter II, Review of Research Projects and Design Synthesis: De Grano et al. (2025), An Arduino-Based Automated Chicken Feeder for Layers Chicken in Macasaet Poultry Farm at Barangay San Gregorio, Alaminos, Laguna.
slides.notes: A closely related project by De Grano et al. (2025), entitled An Arduino-Based Automated Chicken Feeder for Layers Chicken in Macasaet Poultry Farm at Barangay San Gregorio Alaminos, Laguna, also demonstrated the application of automation in poultry feeding. Their system integrated an Arduino Mega 2560, RTC module, ultrasonic sensor, motorized dispensing mechanism, and LCD with a keypad to support scheduled and manual feeding, feed-level monitoring, and timed water distribution. This study provided a relevant reference for the development of HyFePoul's automated feeding and monitoring functions. HyFePoul incorporates a load cell and HX711 amplifier to measure the feed collected in the weighing container and control dispensing based on a configured target weight. Furthermore, HyFePoul provides access through a 7-inch Nextion touchscreen display and a mobile application connected through an ESP32. Its water monitoring mechanism also uses float switches to detect water-level conditions and provide notifications, rather than relying on timed water distribution. These differences demonstrate how HyFePoul builds upon the existing automated poultry-feeding approach by integrating direct feed-weight measurement, additional user access options, and water-level status monitoring.

slides.notes: As shown in Figure 4.35, it illustrates the unsuccessful attempts during the development and configuration of the Nextion Display. The developers encountered a memory overflow error after editing the main user interface under an incorrect device ID and switching to the intended device model. Additionally, firmware uploading failed when using a 128GB microSD card, which exceeded the display's supported hardware limit. These issues prevented the successful transfer and proper configuration of the interface. As shown in Figure 4.36, it presents the successful configuration and firmware uploading of the Nextion Display after addressing the encountered issues. The developers optimized the interface assets to fit the display's available memory and used a compatible microSD card with a capacity below 32GB. Through these adjustments, the firmware was successfully uploaded, allowing the Nextion Display to operate with the intended user interface. Figure 4.37 presents the successful compilation of the Arduino Mega 2560 program using the Arduino IDE. The output indicates that the program occupies 27% of the available program storage and utilizes 56% of the dynamic memory. This confirms that the developed firmware fits within the microcontroller's available memory, allowing the developers to proceed with uploading and testing the programmed system functionalities. As shown in Figure 4.38, it illustrates the successful compilation of the ESP32 program using the Arduino IDE. The output shows that the firmware utilizes 88% of the available program storage and 15% of the dynamic memory. These results confirm that the developed program fits within the ESP32's memory capacity, allowing the developers to proceed with firmware uploading and testing its wireless communication functions.

slides.notes: Table 4.6 presents the results of testing the chain-driven hopper movement and limit switch functionality along the five feeding trays. The chain-driven mechanism successfully moved the hopper across all five trays during the feeding cycle, demonstrating its ability to distribute feed along the designated path. The home and end limit switches also successfully detected the hopper's starting and ending positions, as verified through the corresponding signal changes monitored using the Arduino Mega's Serial Monitor. Upon reaching the ending position, the motor automatically stopped its forward movement and initiated the hopper's return toward its home position. Once the hopper reached its designated home position, the home limit switch was activated, causing the motor to stop its return movement. Furthermore, repeated feeding cycles demonstrated consistent hopper movement, accurate limit switch detection, and proper motor stopping and return operations. Overall, the results demonstrate that the chain-driven hopper mechanism can successfully travel along the five feeding trays, detect its designated movement limits, prevent movement beyond its intended positions, and automatically return to its home position after completing each feeding cycle.

slides.title: Conclusions
slides.lead: The developed device successfully performed the following functions:
items: Feed 3 times per day with a user specified amount of food, as set either via the Nextion interface or mobile application. Feed times and amounts are retained by the device in the event of power failure.

Food is distributed to 5 feeding trays via the chain driven feeding hopper. The feeding starts and ends at specific points as determined by the home and end limit switches. These also prevent the feeding hopper from going above the defined limit, and return it to the home position after feeding.

A user-defined amount of food is distributed to each feeding tray. Each feeding tray has a load cell weighing 1kg attached (total of 5 load cells) and connected to HX711 amplifiers in the control box. Once each feeding tray reaches its desired weight, it will no longer dispense.

The amount of food in the storage hopper is monitored using an ultrasonic sensor. When the food is at a low amount, the user will be sent a notification on the mobile application and the buzzer will sound. If the hopper is almost empty, no feeding will occur, or if feeding is already occurring, feeding will stop.
The amount of water in the gravity fed tank is monitored using a floating switch. If more water needs to be manually added, the buzzer will beep and notifications will be sent to the mobile app.
slides.notes: Based on the accuracy of the results from the gathered data, the following conclusions were drawn:

slides.title: Conclusions
items: Operational status, weights of food in each tray, amount of food in hopper, water status and feeding times are displayed on the Nextion display. Manual feeding routines can also be started from the device. The latest operation data can also be viewed.

A mobile application has been produced so authorised users can login and connect to the device. It allows users to see live data and previous data, view the log data in Google Sheets, change feeding times, and start manual feed routines. Users receive notifications for low food, low water, feeding issues, sensor issues, and if the device is disconnected.

Weighs of food in each tray, amount of food in hopper, water status and alerts from the system have been logged in Firebase Realtime Databases. These are regularly copied to monthly operation logs in Google Sheets, which can be accessed via the mobile application. Feeding times, calibration values for each tray, and total daily food amounts are stored locally in the event of power failures.

Data from the device is sent to the cloud database via the ESP32 using Wi-Fi to ensure the mobile application is updated quickly. In the event of disconnection, feeding times and safety features will still function. Once re-connected, any delays in alerts and daily data will be synchronised.

A back-up power source (battery) is included in the device. In the event of a power failure, the battery can power the entire system. Local feeding, monitoring, display and safety mechanisms can still occur in the absence of internet connection.
after: The device was highly accepted by CpE practitioners, while farmers and the San Pablo City veterinarian official under the ISO 25010 characteristic of functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, interaction capability, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility and safety.

The deployment plan of the Poultry Management System with Weight-Based Feed Dispensing and Water Level Monitoring Device in a poultry farm at Barangay Del Remedio, San Pablo City, Laguna was successful. After the completion of the tasks outlined in the deployment plan, the poultry owner signed an acceptance letter endorsing the design project proposal created by the developers.

slides.title: Recommendations
items: Encourage automated feeding with feed and water monitoring in Barangay Del Remedio, to lessen manual work and feed waste.
Give farmers hands-on training, set-up, user, technical and troubleshooting manuals, and ongoing support.
items2: A sensor that counts the eggs passing under the feeder.
An egg sorting system that sorts eggs by weight.
A lid on the feed outlet that opens and closes around dispensing, so falling feed does not spoil the weight.
Higher-quality load cells for more precise weighing.
A water sensor that reads the level as a percentage, such as an ultrasonic non-contact or submersible pressure sensor.
